page.title: React with TypeScript Interview Questions
page.description: Typing props, children, state, refs and events, why React.FC fell out of favour, generic components and typed reducers.

intro.text: Most React jobs are TypeScript jobs now, so these come up even when the advert does not mention them. The good news is that the questions are narrow: interviewers want to see that you can type a component, a hook and an event handler without reaching for `any`, and that you know why the ergonomics are the way they are.

questions.question: How do you type a component's props?
questions.shortAnswer: Declare a type or interface for the props object and annotate the destructured parameter. That is all React needs — the return type is inferred.

answer.text: Prefer a union of string literals over `string` for anything with a fixed set of values. `variant: 'primary' | 'ghost'` catches a typo at compile time; `variant: string` catches nothing.

followUps: Should the props type be exported?

questions.question: Should you use type or interface for props?
questions.shortAnswer: Either works. Interfaces can be merged and extended and give slightly nicer errors for object shapes; type aliases can express unions, intersections and mapped types. Most teams pick one for consistency, and type is the more common default in React code.

items: `interface` supports declaration merging, which is useful for augmenting a library's types and unwelcome in application code where two definitions silently combining is a bug.
`type` is required when the props are a union, for example a discriminated union of two variants of the same component.
Both support extension: `interface A extends B` and `type A = B & { ... }`.

answer.caption: A shape a plain interface cannot express.

followUps: When could you not use an interface?

questions.question: How do you type children?
questions.shortAnswer: Use React.ReactNode, which covers elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null and undefined. Use React.ReactElement only when the child must be a single element.

answer.text: `ReactNode` is the right default. `JSX.Element` is narrower than people expect and rejects a string child, which is usually not what you want.

followUps: What is the difference between `ReactNode` and `JSX.Element`?

questions.question: What is React.FC and why do many teams avoid it?
questions.shortAnswer: React.FC is a type for function components that annotates the whole function rather than its props. Teams moved away from it because it used to add an implicit children prop, it complicates generic components, and annotating the parameter is simpler.

items: Before React 18's types, `React.FC` added `children` to every component, so a component that accepted no children still typed as if it did. That is fixed, but the habit stuck.
A generic component cannot be expressed cleanly with `React.FC` without awkward casts.
Annotating the parameter gives the same safety with less indirection.

answer.text: It is not wrong to use it, and a codebase that already does should stay consistent. This question is really about whether you can explain a convention rather than just follow one.

followUps: What changed in the React 18 type definitions?

questions.question: How do you type useState, and when is the type argument needed?
questions.shortAnswer: TypeScript infers the type from the initial value, so most calls need no annotation. You need the type argument when the initial value does not represent the full range, typically null or an empty array.

answer.text: `useState([])` infers `never[]`, so the first `setItems([item])` fails to compile. It is the most common TypeScript-and-React confusion, and worth naming explicitly.

followUps: Why does an empty array infer `never[]`?

questions.question: How do you type an event handler?
questions.shortAnswer: Use React's generic event types parameterised by the element: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>. Inline handlers usually infer these for you.

answer.text: The element type argument is what makes `event.target.value` type as `string` rather than erroring. Getting this wrong is the reason people reach for `any` here, so being specific about it is a good signal.

questions.question: How do you type useRef?
questions.shortAnswer: For a DOM node use useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null), which gives a read-only current that may be null. For a mutable value use useRef<number | undefined>(undefined), which gives a writable current.

answer.text: The two overloads behave differently on purpose: passing `null` as the initial value and a DOM type produces a `RefObject`, whose `current` React owns; anything else produces a `MutableRefObject` you can assign to.

followUps: Why is `current` read-only in one case and not the other?

questions.question: How do you type a component that accepts all the native props of an element?
questions.shortAnswer: Extend the element's prop type from React's JSX intrinsic elements, or use ComponentPropsWithoutRef, then add your own props on top and spread the rest onto the element.

answer.text: Use `ComponentPropsWithRef` when the component forwards a ref. The pattern matters for design systems: consumers get `aria-*`, `data-*`, `type`, `disabled` and every other native attribute without you enumerating them.

followUps: How would you type this if the component could render as an anchor instead?

questions.question: How do you write a generic component?
questions.shortAnswer: Declare a type parameter on the function and use it in the props, so the caller's data type flows through to the callbacks and the rendered items.

answer.text: In a `.tsx` file, `<T>` on an arrow function is parsed as JSX. Use a function declaration, or write `<T,>` with the trailing comma to disambiguate.

followUps: Why does the trailing comma matter?

questions.question: How do you type useReducer and its actions?
questions.shortAnswer: Model the actions as a discriminated union on a type field and type the reducer as (state: State, action: Action) => State. TypeScript then narrows the payload inside each case and errors on an unhandled action.

answer.text: With the return type annotated and no `default` case, TypeScript reports a missing branch when a new action is added, which turns the reducer into a checklist that maintains itself.

questions.question: How should you type data coming back from an API?
questions.shortAnswer: Do not assert it. A response is unknown until something checks it, so validate it at the boundary with a schema library such as Zod and let the validated type flow inwards.

answer.text: `const user = (await response.json()) as User` is a lie the compiler believes. If the API changes, you get a runtime crash somewhere far away instead of an error at the boundary.

followUps: What is the difference between `unknown` and `any`?
Where should validation live in the app?
